hints: Look at what changes in step 2, the $\text{-Cl}$ on $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCl}$ is replaced by $\text{-CN}$ to give $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCN}$, so think about which ion can act as the nucleophile to supply $\text{CN}$.
walkthrough:
Spot the substitution pattern**
You start with $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCl}$ and you end with $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCN}$. The $\text{C=O}$ core stays exactly the same, only the $\text{-Cl}$ leaving group is swapped for $\text{-CN}$. That is classic nucleophilic substitution at a very reactive acyl chloride.

Choose the cyanide source**
To supply $\text{CN}^{-}$, you use an ionic cyanide salt such as potassium cyanide or sodium cyanide. The $\text{CN}^{-}$ attacks the carbonyl carbon, $\text{Cl}^{-}$ leaves, and you extend the carbon skeleton ready for hydrolysis in step 3.
Final answer: Reagent for step 2: $\text{KCN}$ or $\text{NaCN}$ or $\text{CN}^{-}$.

hints: For step 1, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COOH}$ to $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCl}$, recall the three standard chlorinating agents that replace $\text{-OH}$ by $\text{-Cl}$ without touching the $\text{C=O}$.

For step 4, a keto-acid $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCOOH}$ becomes a hydroxy-acid $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)COOH}$, so identify which mild hydride reduces a ketone $\text{C=O}$ to $\text{CH-OH}$ but leaves a carboxylic acid unchanged.
walkthrough:
Make the acyl chloride in step 1**
Think of $\text{-OH}$ as a poor leaving group. You need to swap it for $\text{-Cl}$. The A Level reagents for $\text{RCOOH}$ to $\text{RCOCl}$ are $\text{PCl}_{5}$, $\text{SOCl}_{2}$, or $\text{PCl}_{3}$ with heat. Any one of these gives $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCl}$ cleanly.

Reduce only the ketone in step 4**
Now look closely at $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCOOH}$. It has a ketone $\text{C=O}$ next to a carboxylic acid $\text{COOH}$. The product keeps the $\text{COOH}$ intact but the ketone becomes $\text{CH-OH}$. That calls for the selective reducing agent $\text{NaBH}_{4}$, which reduces aldehydes and ketones but not carboxylic acids. Do not use $\text{LiAlH}_{4}$ here because it would also reduce the acid.

Final answer: step 1: $\text{PCl}_{3}$ with heat or $\text{PCl}_{5}$ or $\text{SOCl}_{2}$
step 4: $\text{NaBH}_{4}$

hints: In R, $\text{H}_{2}\text{N-CH(CH}_{3}\text{)CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{-COCl}$, the $\text{NH}_{2}$ end can attack its own $\text{COCl}$ end on warming, so count the atoms that will close to form a ring and work out the molecular formula $\text{C}_{5}\text{H}_{9}\text{NO}$.

$\text{LiAlH}_{4}$ in step II reduces the $\text{C=O}$ of an amide to $\text{CH}_{2}$ while leaving the rest of the ring intact, so think how S changes when $\text{-CONH-}$ becomes $\text{-CH}_{2}\text{NH-}$.
walkthrough:
Let R curl up on itself**
Draw R out: $\text{H}_{2}\text{N-CH(CH}_{3}\text{)-CH}_{2}\text{-CH}_{2}\text{-C(=O)-Cl}$. You have a nucleophile ($\text{-NH}_{2}$) and a superb electrophile ($\text{-COCl}$) in the same molecule. On warming they meet. The N lone pair attacks the $\text{C=O}$ carbon, $\text{Cl}^{-}$ leaves, and $\text{HCl}$ is lost. Count round: N plus 4 carbons gives a 5-membered ring.

Draw S as a cyclic amide**
The ring is a lactam: a cyclic amide. At the top you have $\text{C(=O)-NH-}$, then $\text{-CH(CH}_{3}\text{)-CH}_{2}\text{-CH}_{2}\text{-}$ back to the carbonyl. That is 5-methylpyrrolidin-2-one, formula $\text{C}_{5}\text{H}_{9}\text{NO}$. The $\text{CH}_{3}$ sits on the carbon next to N.

Reduce the amide to the amine for T**
$\text{LiAlH}_{4}$ is the strong hydride that reduces $\text{-CONH-}$ to $\text{-CH}_{2}\text{NH-}$. So the $\text{C=O}$ in S becomes $\text{CH}_{2}$. The ring size and the methyl substituent do not change. You get 2-methylpyrrolidine, a cyclic secondary amine with N-H.

Final answer: S: 5-methylpyrrolidin-2-one, a 5-membered ring containing $\text{-CO-NH-}$ with $\text{CH}_{3}$ on the carbon adjacent to N.
T: 2-methylpyrrolidine, a 5-membered ring containing $\text{-CH}_{2}\text{-NH-}$ with $\text{CH}_{3}$ on the carbon adjacent to N.

hints: In step I a small molecule $\text{HCl}$ is eliminated as the ring closes from $\text{R}$ to $\text{S}$, so recall the name given to reactions that join two groups with loss of a small molecule.
In step II $\text{LiAlH}_{4}$ converts $\text{C=O}$ to $\text{CH}_{2}$ with gain of hydrogen, so recall the general reaction type for gain of hydrogen or loss of oxygen.
walkthrough:
Classify step I**
An amine plus an acyl chloride normally gives an amide plus $\text{HCl}$. Here it happens intramolecularly to close the ring, but the principle is identical. Joining with elimination of a small molecule such as $\text{HCl}$ or $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ is condensation. It is also nucleophilic addition-elimination, but the required label here is condensation.

Classify step II**
$\text{LiAlH}_{4}$ delivers hydride to the carbonyl carbon. The $\text{C=O}$ loses oxygen in effect and gains hydrogen to become $\text{CH}_{2}$. Gain of hydrogen is reduction, so step II is reduction of the amide to an amine.

Final answer: step I: condensation
step II: reduction

hints: Monomer R contains both $\text{-NH}_{2}$ and $\text{-COCl}$ so it can react with itself head to tail, think about which linkage forms when $\text{-NH}_{2}$ meets $\text{-COCl}$ and what small molecule is lost.

To show two repeat units, write the $\text{-NH-CH(CH}_{3}\text{)CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{-CO-}$ block twice in a row with continuation bonds through the ends, keeping the amide $\text{CO-NH}$ connections correct.
walkthrough:
Recognise a self-condensing monomer**
R is $\text{H}_{2}\text{N-CH(CH}_{3}\text{)CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{-COCl}$. One end is an amine, the other is an acyl chloride. The $\text{NH}_{2}$ of one molecule attacks the $\text{COCl}$ of the next, eliminating $\text{HCl}$ each time. Repeating this gives a polyamide with $\text{-CO-NH-}$ links, exactly like nylon chemistry but from a single monomer.

Build two linked repeats correctly**
Write the hydrocarbon skeleton in order: $\text{-N(H)-CH(CH}_{3}\text{)-CH}_{2}\text{-CH}_{2}\text{-C(=O)-}$. Then join a second identical block to it through the amide bond: $\text{-C(=O)-N(H)-}$. Show exactly two of these blocks, put short continuation bonds sticking out at the left N end and the right C=O end, and keep every $\text{CH}_{3}$, $\text{CH}_{2}$ and $\text{NH}$ in the right place. That earns both marks for amide bond, correct hydrocarbon portions, two units and continuation bonds.

Final answer: Polyamide: $\text{-[NH-CH(CH}_{3}\text{)CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{-C(=O)]-}$ shown with exactly two repeat units, e.g. $\text{-[NH-CH(CH}_{3}\text{)CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{C(=O)-NH-CH(CH}_{3}\text{)CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{C(=O)]-}$ with continuation bonds at both ends.
